\begin{center}
{\Large\bfseries Impossible Maths I}\\Sheet 3 --- MT18\\First topic questions
\end{center}


\begin{enumerate}

\item \begin{enumerate}
  \item Define what it means for a finite subset of a vector space to be
  {\em linearly independent}, a {\em spanning set}, and a {\em basis}.

  State the {\it Steinitz Exchange Lemma}.

  Prove that if a vector space $V$ has a finite basis, then every linearly
  independent subset of $V$ may be extended to a basis.

  Prove that any two finite bases of a vector space have the same number of
  elements. Define the {\em dimension} of a finite-dimensional vector space.

  \item Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space.

  Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are subspaces of $V$.

  Prove that
  \[ \dim(X+Y)+\dim(X\cap Y)=\dim X+\dim Y. \]

  \item Suppose $V$ is a finite-dimensional vector space, and $T:V\to V $
  is a linear transformation. Suppose that for all $v\in V$, if $T(T(v))=0$,
  then $T(v)=0$. Prove that $V=\ker T\oplus \mathop{\rm im} T$, and that the
  restriction, $T{\restriction} {\mathop{\rm im} T}$, of $T$ to $\mathop{\rm
    im} T$ is a bijection from $\mathop{\rm im} T$ to itself.

  [{\em You may assume the Rank-Nullity Theorem.}]

  [{\em If\/ $V$ and $W$ are vector spaces, $T:V\to W$ is a linear
    transformation,

    and $U$ is a subspace of $V$, then we define the {\em restriction}
    $T{\restriction} U$ of $T$ to $U$ to be a linear transformation from $U$
    to $W$ such that for all $u\in U$, $(T{\restriction} U)(u)=T(u)$.}]
\end{enumerate}



\item \begin{enumerate}
  \item Define an {\em elementary row operation}, and say what it means
  for a matrix to be in {\em row-reduced echelon form}. Describe how any
  matrix may be reduced to row-reduced echelon form.

  \item For which values of $\lambda$ is the following system of equat
  ions solvable? In each case calculate the solutions.
  \[\begin{array}{ccccc}x&+2y&-3z&=&5 \\ x&-2y&-5z&=&7 \\ 2x&+8y&+(-\lambda-6)z&=&8 \\ x&-2y&+(\lambda-3)z&=&\lambda^2+3\end{array}\]
\end{enumerate}




\item \begin{enumerate}
  \item \begin{enumerate}
    \item Define what it means to say that a square matrix with real
    entries is {\em diagonalisable} over ${\mathbb R}$.  \item Show that
    if $A$ is a square matrix with real entries and $\bf u$ and $\bf v$ are
    eigenvalues of $A$ corresponding to different eigenvalues, then $\bf u$
    and $\bf v$ are linearly independent.
  \end{enumerate}

  \item \begin{enumerate}
    \item Consider the $2\times 2$ real square matrix
    \[ A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\cr b&d\cr\end{pmatrix}. \] Show that $A$ has at
    least one real eigenvalue; and that if $a\neq d$ or $b\neq 0$, then it
    has two distinct real eigenvalues.

    Deduce that $A$ is diagonalisable.

    \item Determine the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ for which the real
    matrix
    \[ A=\begin{pmatrix}1&\alpha\cr \beta&1\cr\end{pmatrix} \] is
    diagonalisable.

    \item Determine when the $2\times 2$ real matrix
    \[ A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\cr c&a\cr\end{pmatrix} \] is diagonalisable.
  \end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}



\item Let $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ be vectors in
$\mathbb{R}^3$.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item 
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item Prove that $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are linearly
    independent if and only if 
    $\mathbf{u}.(\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{w})\neq \mathbf{0}$.  
    \item Establish the identity
    \[
    \mathbf{u}\mathbin{\land}(\mathbf{w}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{v})
    =(\mathbf{u}.\mathbf{v})\mathbf{w}-(\mathbf{u}.\mathbf{w})\mathbf{v}.
    \]
  \end{enumerate}

  \item  Prove that $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are linearly
  independent if and only if
  $\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{w}$, 
  $\mathbf{w}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{u}$, and
  $\mathbf{u}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{v}$ are linearly independent.

  \item  Suppose that $\mathbf{u}$, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are
  linearly independent, and that
  \[ \mathbf{r}=a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{v}+c\mathbf{w}. \]
  Find coefficients $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ such that
  \[
  \mathbf{r}=\alpha\mathbf{v}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{w}
  +\beta\mathbf{w}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{u}
  +\gamma\mathbf{u}\mathbin{\land}\mathbf{v}.
  \]

\end{enumerate}



\end{enumerate}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We study the ${\mathcal M}$-closed validation of a generative model $q$ against a
target $p$ over the space ${\mathcal X}$. Conformal calibration turns a weak plug-in
classifier into a powerful two-sample test with finite-sample type-I control.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
A popular tool for evaluating generative models is the classifier two-sample
test (C2ST). It reframes distributional comparison between $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ as
a classification task over the space ${\mathcal X}$, with the Bayes-optimal classifier
bisecting $\mathbb{R}^2$ between the two means.

\paragraph{Summary of contributions.} We introduce the Conformal C2ST and give
a robustness theory for weak classifiers. We show that conformal calibration
decouples type-I error control from discriminative accuracy.

\paragraph{A toy example.} Consider ${\mathcal N}(\mathbf{0}, I_2)$ versus a mean shift,
so that $q$ is ${\mathcal N}([0.5, 0]^\top, I_2)$. The rank statistic
\[
  r = \sum_{i=1}^{M} {\mathbb I}\{\theta \le \tilde\theta_i\}
\]
is uniform over $\{0, 1, \dots, M\}$ when $q$ matches $p$.

\section{Robustness of the uniform test}
Let ${\mathcal O}$ denote an oracle and write the conformal $p$-value as a function of
the score. We control the variance $\text{Var}[r]$ and the expectation $\mathbb{E}[r]$ of
the rank statistic under the null.

\begin{theorem}[Decoupling]
\label{thm:decouple}
For any plug-in classifier with score $s$, the conformal calibration map
satisfies
\[
  \Big| \mathbb{E}\big[ \phi(s) \big] - \alpha \Big| \le \left\| {s - s^\star} \right\|
  \xrightarrow{\;n \to \infty\;} 0 ,
\]
where $s^\star$ is the Bayes-optimal score and $\left| {\alpha} \right| \le 1$.
\end{theorem}

As shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:decouple}, the conformal test maintains validity
even when the classifier is weak, since the ranking signal
$\overset{\text{rank}}{\longrightarrow}$ aggregates across draws.

\section{Introduction}
\subsection{Legendre Polynomials}
Let $P_k(x)$ be the degree $k$ Legendre polynomial. The Legendre polynomials
are an orthogonal family of polynomials on $[-1,1]$ that obey the orthogonality
relation
$$
\int_{-1}^1 P_j(x) P_k(x) dx = 0,
$$
for $j \not = k$. The first few Legendre polynomials are
$$
P_0(x) = 1, \qquad P_1(x) = x, \qquad \text{and} \qquad P_2(x) = \frac{3 x^2 - 1}{2}.  
$$
The Legendre polynomials obey the recurrence relation
$$
(k+1) P_{k+1}(x) = (2 k + 1) x P_k(x) - k P_{k-1}(x),
$$
the differential equation
$$
(1 - x^2) P_k''(x) - 2 x P_k'(x) + k(k+1) P_k(x) = 0,
$$
for $k \ge 1$.
